Seasonality is often smoother than a week-by-week categorical effect. `fourier(week, n=3, period=52)` represents a yearly cycle with three sine/cosine harmonic pairs, each with its own coefficient. Unlike a transform, the basis owns all six weights, so it is written without a `beta*` prefix.

## Simulate one seasonal cycle

::: {#1f59f378 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

import pathmc

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
week = np.arange(104, dtype=float)
seasonal_signal = 2 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * week / 52) + 0.6 * np.cos(4 * np.pi * week / 52)
df = pd.DataFrame({"week": week, "sales": 10 + seasonal_signal + rng.normal(0, 0.25, len(week))})

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
ax.plot(df["week"], df["sales"], ".", alpha=0.5, label="observed sales")
ax.plot(df["week"], 10 + seasonal_signal, color="C1", label="seasonal signal")
ax.set(xlabel="week", ylabel="sales")
ax.legend()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](fourier_seasonality_files/figure-html/cell-2-output-1.png){width=660 height=283}

## Build the seasonal model

::: {#7b7de0aa .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
model = pathmc.model("sales ~ fourier(week, n=3, period=52)", data=df)
model.equations()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=2}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta_{sales} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=0,\, sigma=10) \\
\sigma_{sales} &\sim \text{HalfNormal}(sigma=1) \\
\beta_{fourier,sales,week} &\sim \text{Normal}(mu=0,\, sigma=1)
\\[6pt]
\mu_{sales} &= \beta_{0,\,sales} + f_{\mathrm{fourier}}(\mathrm{week}) \\
\mathrm{sales} &\sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{sales},\, \sigma_{sales})
\end{aligned}
$$
:::
:::


::: {#29d774af .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
idata = model.fit(draws=200, tune=200, chains=1, cores=1, progressbar=False, random_seed=42)
new_year = model.do(set={"week": np.arange(104, 208, dtype=float)}, kind="mean")
new_year.mean("sales")
```

The basis is also valid when its input is a latent mediator, because sine and cosine are constructed in the PyMC graph. `do()` therefore recomputes the harmonic contribution when it changes the input, without an HSGP-style fitted support boundary. See [Basis Terms](../../user_guide/12b-basis-terms.qmd) for the capability table and comparison with `hsgp()`.
